content: Presenilin-associated rhomboid-like protein (PARL) is a mitochondrial inner membrane protein encoded by the PARL gene located on chromosome 3 in humans. It belongs to the rhomboid family of intramembrane serine proteases. This protein plays a critical role in signal transduction, apoptosis, neurodegenerative diseases, and type 2 diabetes. Structure Members of the rhomboid family share a conserved core structure consisting of six transmembrane helices (TMHs). The catalytic dyad, formed by serine and histidine residues, is embedded within TMH-4 and TMH-6, respectively. This dyad is located deep below the membrane surface, indicating that peptide bond hydrolysis occurs within the hydrophobic phospholipid bilayer. As a member of the PARL subfamily, PARL contains an additional N-terminal transmembrane helix, which may form a loop connecting to the catalytic core. Function The PARL gene encodes a mitochondrial integral membrane protein. After proteolytic processing, a small peptide known as P-beta is generated and translocated to the nucleus. PARL is involved in signal transduction through regulated intramembrane proteolysis of membrane-tethered precursor proteins. Variations in the PARL gene have been associated with an increased risk of type 2 diabetes. Alternative splicing of this gene results in multiple transcript variants encoding different isoforms. PARL also plays a role in apoptosis through its interactions with mitochondrial GTPase optic atrophy 1 (OPA1) and the Bcl-2 family-related protein HAX1. OPA1 primarily regulates mitochondrial fusion within the inner mitochondrial membrane. However, after proteolytic cleavage by PARL, the short soluble form of OPA1 inhibits apoptosis by slowing the release of cytochrome c, thereby reducing pro-apoptotic signaling. Alternatively, PARL can inhibit apoptosis by coordinating with HAX1 to activate the HtrA2 protease, which prevents the accumulation of the pro-apoptotic protein Bax. Mutations in the S77N variant of PARL are not a common cause of early-onset Parkinson’s disease. However, variations in the sequence or expression of presenilin-associated rhomboid-like protein (PSARL) may represent a novel risk factor for type 2 diabetes and other components of metabolic syndrome. Mutations in PARL may also contribute to Leber hereditary optic neuropathy by disrupting normal mitochondrial function, leading to retinal ganglion cell death and neurodegeneration. Interactions PARL has been shown to interact with the following proteins: PINK1 (PTEN-induced kinase 1), OPA1 (optic atrophy 1), and HAX1 (HCLS1-associated protein X-1).
